chapter_theme: The maiden-city is built and the Vidyadhara maiden enters it; Maruci reports to the king of Suramai, who orders the city dressed and, on his counsellors' word that the Vidyadhara lord is an equal, has elephants, chariots, horses and soldiers made ready while the prince orders gifts of cloth, jewels, drink and food sent to the Vidyadhara city.

cast.role: those who raise the maiden-city; named only by a plural verb
the Vidyadhara king's daughter, called only 'maiden' here
the learned Vidyadhara envoy who goes to the king
the king of the Suramai land and Podanam, named only by royal titles here
the garland-chested prince, taken to be Tivittan, who orders the procession and gifts
the elephant-drivers who ready the war-elephants
the soldiers who say life is taken only by fate
the official told to send cloth, jewels, drink and food to the Vidyadhara city

899.reading: In the guarded grove round the old fort the builders raise a great maiden-city for the girl, with many maidens keeping its gate.
899.nuance: Every line opens with the same word கன்னி, in a yamaka that plays on 'maiden' and 'city of the maiden'; the exact sense of each use is held loosely.
899.event: Builders raise a great city for the Vidyadhara maiden in the guarded grove.

900.reading: The maiden steps down from her lightning-bright aerial car while golden women praise her and, by her father's grace, enters the jewelled mansion of the maiden-city.
900.event: The Vidyadhara maiden descends from the aerial car and enters the maiden-city.

901.reading: Once the party is settled, Maruci goes to the king of the river-watered Suramai land, bows at his feet and tells him, and the victorious king swells with gladness.
901.nuance: The king of Suramai is taken to be Pirasapathi of Podanam; the verse does not name him.
901.event: Maruci reports the Vidyadhara party's arrival to the king, who is delighted.

902.reading: The king orders the jewelled ornaments worn, the drums sounded through the city, arches raised in every direction and full golden pots set out.
902.nuance: The speaker is not named in the verse and is taken from the king's joy in 901.
902.event: The king orders the city dressed and drummed for the wedding.

903.reading: The king orders that the needy seize two treasures, that neighbouring kings be summoned by envoys, and that the temples of the Jina's wealthy city hold a festival.
903.nuance: The wedding is made a public gift-day for beggars and a political summons to neighbouring kings together; the closing words about rain are obscure.
903.event: The king orders wealth given out, kings summoned and a festival held.

904.reading: The king orders the women to adorn the bright-jewelled girl for her going into the jewelled grove, with bright ear-rings, ornaments and finery.
904.nuance: Whether the one to be adorned is the Vidyadhara maiden or the bride-to-be of the line is held loosely; the verse says only 'the woman of the gem-grove'.
904.event: The king orders the maiden dressed for her entry into the grove.

905.reading: The king orders the elephants with their women to go in, the young cow-elephants to be made ready, and the fire-armed troops to enter and keep guard.
905.event: The king orders elephants, women and guard troops to take their posts.

906.reading: Having ordered the attendants so, the king speaks to Maruci in words meant to bewilder him and bids him enter a golden-city mansion.
906.nuance: The sense of the king's words to Maruci turns on one rare word and a doubtful construction.
906.event: The king speaks to Maruci and sends him to lodge in a golden mansion.

907.reading: The king, gracious to the envoy's side, asks his gathered counsellors how the capable Vidyadhara lord is to be met, and they answer in a way the king understands.
907.event: The king asks his counsellors how to receive the Vidyadhara lord and they answer.

908.reading: The counsellors tell the king that the Vidyadhara lord was born in a great sea of noble kin, that his link to Nami's line also draws near, and that there is no fault in him to count.
908.nuance: 'Nami' in line 3 is taken to be the ancestor of the Vidyadhara line whose song is told in an earlier sarukkam; the verse's grammar is clipped.
908.event: The counsellors vouch for the Vidyadhara lord's lineage.

909.reading: The counsellors add that he matches the king in clan, character and beauty, is strong beyond challenge, and has the build of a wrestler with pillar-like shoulders.
909.event: The counsellors praise the Vidyadhara lord's equality with the king.

910.reading: Therefore, say the counsellors, whatever the king does for him brings no blame; they speak as men who are a sea of the treatise on conduct.
910.nuance: The counsellors are called a sea of the treatise on conduct (நீதிநூல்) in the narrator's voice; the verse does not say whom the treatise belongs to.
910.event: The counsellors advise that no fault attaches to any honour done to the Vidyadhara lord.

claims.claim: a ruler may spend freely on an ally who equals him in birth and virtue, and no blame attaches

911.reading: Hearing them, the king rejoices that his counsellors are men of wisdom and goes through the gold gate kept by flower-eared women to the courtyard of the garlanded prince's fine palace.
911.nuance: The garlanded prince is taken to be Tivittan, the groom; the verse names him only by his garland.
911.event: The king goes to the prince's palace courtyard.

912.reading: He orders ready the war-elephants, whose rut falls like rain, with diamond goads and chains planted firm, and the chariots and horses.
912.nuance: The speaker is taken to be the prince, but the king is also a possible subject of 'என்றான்'.
912.event: The prince orders elephants, chariots and horses made ready.

913.reading: Hearing the order, the drivers loose the elephants from the post-chains, take off the foot-fetters, tie girth cloths and ready them, and stand by with banners raised.
913.nuance: The printed stanza ran to eight half-lines in the source; the editor's join does not change the sense here.
913.event: The drivers unchain and equip the war-elephants for the procession.

914.reading: The firm chariots, with golden shields, gem-set floors and golden finials on their fronts, come up with banners flying, as if the shaking earth were taking them for a bangle.
914.nuance: The poet's conceit is that the earth shakes under the chariots as if wearing them as a wrist-bangle.
914.event: The decked chariots arrive with their banners.

915.reading: The fighting horses are decked with golden face-plates, strings of gems, auspicious trappings and golden-tasselled whisks.

916.reading: Soldiers with fastened anklets, girded sashes and blazing swords gather round, men whose declaration that life should be taken only by the fate fastened to it makes even Death tremble.
916.nuance: The warriors' words set fate (ஊழ்) as the only legitimate killer, which makes their swords restrained; the verse's grammar is clipped and the exact subject of 'tremble' is held loosely.
916.event: The soldiers gather round, declaring that only bound fate may take a life.

claims.claim: a life may be taken only by the fate that is bound to it, and by nothing else

917.reading: When the host is ready, the prince calls Maruci, who stands beside the king and counsellors, to come, seats him on a golden-browed elephant and, standing before him with a loving smile, speaks.
917.nuance: The subject of the verb is taken to be the prince, who gives the next orders.
917.event: The prince calls Maruci, seats him on an elephant and speaks to him.

918.reading: The garland-chested prince calls Chitradharan and bids him spread cotton, silk and cloths and fill the tall city of the Vidyadhara of unfailing might with gem ornaments.
918.event: The prince orders Chitradharan to send cloth and jewels to the Vidyadhara city.

919.reading: The prince bids the heaps of gold ornaments, gem-strings, diamond mountains, right-turned conches and coral be piled before the Vidyadhara king's palace.
919.event: The prince orders gold, gems and coral heaped before the Vidyadhara king's palace.

920.reading: The prince bids the city be stocked with hot honeyed liquor and sweet toddy of every sort so that the guests may be feasted as each desires.
920.event: The prince orders drink stocked to feast the Vidyadhara guests.

921.reading: The prince bids coconuts, tender fruit, ripe-fruit clusters, sugar, leaf bundles and cane sweets be poured into the old city.
921.nuance: Several of the foods named are rare words and held loosely.
921.event: The prince orders fruit and sweets poured into the old city.

922.reading: The prince bids wreaths, scents, flowers, garlands and bells be tied up in bunches and strewn thick through the city's bounds and along its aerial car-streets.
922.nuance: 'வேலோய்' is a vocative to the one ordered; the verse's last half is held loosely.
922.event: The prince orders flowers and garlands strewn through the city's bounds.

links.note: The maiden-city built in 899 is where the maiden lands in 900.
links.teaches: The city is built before she arrives, so her descent into it is a planned reception and not a stray landing.

links.note: Maruci's report in 901 draws the king's reply to him in 906.
links.teaches: The envoy's report wins a lodging and a reply, so the envoy's word is what sets the king's preparations moving.

links.note: The soldiers hold that only bound fate may take a life; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
links.teaches: A warrior class that claims only fate may kill makes its own arms the servants of fate, which the couplet's praise of fate's strength never says.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that fate outruns every other plan, which would explain why soldiers can speak of fate as the only killer.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of armed men who put its claim into their own battle-cry and so make Death tremble.

links.note: The prince stocks the city's feast for guests as each desires; Kural 81 says a household exists to tend guests.
links.teaches: The wedding feast is a state's display and a political courtesy, which shows a limit of the couplet's household hospitality that needs no such display.

gains.a: The verse lacks the moral reason that makes feasting a guest the very point of keeping wealth, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case of hospitality scaled to a royal alliance, where the feast also announces rank and ties.

source_issues: Verse 914: the printed stanza ran into eight half-lines and was repaired to four lines.
Verses 902 to 910: the speakers are not named in the text and are taken from the story so far.
Verses 911 to 922: the garland-chested prince is taken to be Tivittan; the verses never name him, and the speaker of 912 to 917 could be the king.
Verses 903, 904, 906, 907 and 921: several rare words and a broken word division leave the sense held loosely.
